chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
title: How the McShann rhythm section found each other; the guitar player
summary: Influenced by Basie and above all Page, Ramey, McShann and Gus Johnson let the rhythm section walk alone; a guitarist was added in 1941.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Well, when you three got together Jay McShann and jointly shared that Gus, now, what were you -- what were you thinking in terms of, I mean, had you heard -- I mean, were you doing your own thing or were you influenced by Basie, or what?
We were slightly influenced by Basie, and I definitely was influenced by Walter Page.

But we used to have our conferences and talk, and I would express to them what Page had told me, about how we could should team, how that bass drum drummer's foot shouldn't be too heavy, and how the bass player should stay away from trying to run every chord that goes along, but get a straight line where you can push, and Max McShann was naturally talented in how to play with the band, anyway.

We began to find each other, and it was during our first year that lots of times the horns would lay out -- McShann had the horns lay out and the rhythm section and would just walk for maybe five or ten minutes. Just McShann cooking on the piano and --
When did you get the guitar player?
Sometime in late '41, something like that. Now, we had him in 1940, but I don't think he made the
Didn't you need him, or was that just sort of --
I think that was a fill-up. Back in those days, certain halls had to have a certain number of musicians. And I think it was a fill-up, because --
And that's sort of appearance, too, I mean, people are accustomed to seeing a guitar there. I guess if you hadn't got one, they'd think you were --
Yeah, immature, incorrect band or something. But --
